lifecycle.title: The life of a bill, in four words
lifecycle.intro: Every bill in the list carries a status. Read the column top to bottom and you know which bills are still being checked, which are waiting to be paid, and which are settled.

steps.question: Still being checked
steps.body: The bill is entered but not yet accepted. Compare quantities with what arrived and prices with the purchase order while it is still a draft.

steps.question: Accepted, and money is owed
steps.body: You owe the vendor this amount. When you pay part of it, the Paid column shows how much, so a 1,38,000 taka bill with 70,000 paid is easy to spot.

steps.question: Fully paid
steps.body: Paid equals Amount. Nothing more to pay. The bill stays in the list for the record and the audit.

aside.body: Entered by mistake, or replaced by a corrected bill. A voided bill stays in the list with its number, so the numbering has no gaps an auditor would ask about.

lifecycle.formTitle: What you fill in on a new bill

form.label: Project (optional)
form.body: Tag the bill to a project or job if the cost belongs to one.

form.label: Vendor
form.body: Search and pick the supplier. Their details come with the bill.

form.label: Cash account
form.body: Where the payment will come from. Filled in for you (account 1010) unless you choose another.

form.label: Accounts payable
form.body: The account that holds what you owe until you pay. Filled in for you (account 2010).

form.label: Terms
form.body: Payment terms such as On receipt or Net 30. The due date in the list follows from it.

connect.title: A bill sits between buying and paying

items.chequeRegister: When you pay by cheque, with its date, so none is forgotten.
items.bankAccounts: Where the payment leaves from, and the balance to check.
items.pettyCash: Small purchases paid from the cash box, kept apart from bills.
items.vatRegister: The VAT on every bill line, ready for the monthly return.
items.accountingHub: Unpaid bills make up the AP figure.
items.financialReports: Purchases and payables in your statements.

local.title: Bills that follow how suppliers are paid in Bangladesh
local.intro: Suppliers here are often paid in parts, on dates that follow the buyer’s cash flow. The bill keeps every one of those payments in view until the balance reaches zero.

points.title: VAT on purchases, line by line
points.body: Each bill line carries its own VAT rate and amount. It lands in the VAT Register, so purchase VAT is ready when the monthly return is due.

points.title: Part payments, kept in view
points.body: Pay a supplier in two or three instalments. The Paid column grows with each one and the balance is always on the bill.

points.title: Allocate a payment to the right bill
points.body: When one payment covers several bills, allocate it from the row, so each bill shows exactly what was settled.

points.title: Terms that match the supplier
points.body: On receipt for the cement supplier, Net 30 for the packaging vendor. The due date follows the terms you choose.

story.title: One supplier bill, from the gate to paid
story.intro: A sample bill for plastic raw material, the way it usually runs.

steps.text: 40 units of plastic arrive at the gate with the supplier’s bill.
The bill is entered as a draft. The quantity is checked against the purchase order and the VAT against the bill.
Approved. The full 1,38,000 taka now shows as owed to the vendor.
A part payment of 70,000 goes out. Paid shows it, and 68,000 stays due.
The balance is paid on the due date. Paid matches Amount, and the bill turns to paid.

faq.title: Questions we get about bills

items.q: What is a bill in Adon ERP?
items.a: It is a supplier’s invoice that you record: a vendor, a project if there is one, line items with VAT, and payment terms. Once approved, it shows what you owe until you pay it.

items.q: What do draft, approved, paid and void mean?
items.a: Draft is still being checked. Approved means you owe the amount. Paid means the full amount has been paid. Void bills stay in the list with their number, for the record.

items.q: Can I pay a supplier in parts?
items.a: Yes. Use “Record Payment” on the bill. The Paid column shows how much has gone out so far, next to the full amount.

items.q: What does Allocate do?
items.a: It sets a payment against the bill it settles. When one payment covers more than one bill, allocating keeps each bill’s balance right.

items.q: How is VAT handled on a bill?
items.a: Each line has its own VAT rate. The bill shows the VAT amount for every line and adds it to the line total, and the VAT goes to the VAT Register.

items.q: Do I need to choose accounts every time?
items.a: No. The cash account (1010) and the accounts payable account (2010) are filled in automatically. You can change them for a particular bill.

items.q: Can I print and export bills?
items.a: Yes. Print a bill from its row or from the bill itself, and export the list to CSV or Excel.

items.q: Where is Adon ERP available?
items.a: We are currently onboarding companies in Dhaka. Book a demo and we will enter a sample bill and a part payment with you.

closing.title: Bring a supplier bill that is hard to track. We will enter it and pay it in the demo.

lifecycle.title: How a purchase order moves, in three steps
lifecycle.intro: Every order in the list carries a status, and the Received column shows how much of it has arrived. Together they tell you what is still waiting on a supplier.

steps.question: Still being drawn up
steps.body: The order exists but has not been approved. Set the items, quantities and prices while it is still a draft.

steps.question: Approved, goods expected
steps.body: The supplier can now deliver. The PO amount is what you have agreed to pay, and Received stays at zero until goods arrive.

steps.question: Received, ready to bill
steps.body: Received matches the PO amount. Convert the order to a bill, and the bill is checked against what you ordered.

aside.body: Raised by mistake, or replaced by a new order. It stays in the list with its number, so the numbering has no gaps an auditor would ask about.

form.label: PO title

form.label: Vendor

form.label: Order date

form.body: Your own reference or the supplier’s quotation number, so the order can be matched later.

form.label: Items (step 2)
form.body: After the header, add the items with quantity and unit cost. The PO amount is worked out from them.

faq.title: Questions we get about purchase orders

items.q: What is a purchase order in Adon ERP?
items.a: It is a record of what you have agreed to buy from a supplier: a title, a vendor, a date and the items with quantity and unit cost. Once approved, it shows what you expect to receive and pay for.

items.q: What do draft, approved and received mean?
items.a: Draft is still being drawn up. Approved means the order has gone to the supplier. Received means the goods have arrived, and the Received column shows how much.

items.q: What do I need to fill in to create an order?
items.a: Only the PO title is required. Add the vendor, the order date and a reference, then add the items in the second step. The PO amount is worked out from the items.

items.q: How do I turn an order into a bill?
items.a: Open the approved order and click “Convert to Bill”. The items, quantities and VAT come across to the bill.

items.q: Can goods arrive in parts?
items.a: Yes. The Received column shows how much has arrived so far, next to the PO amount, so part deliveries are easy to follow.

items.q: Can I cancel an order?
items.a: Yes. Use “Void”. A voided order stays in the list with its number, for the record.

items.q: Can I export purchase orders?
items.a: Yes. Search the list, then export to CSV or Excel, or print it.

items.a: We are currently onboarding companies in Dhaka. Book a demo and we will raise a sample order and convert it to a bill with you.

ui.title: Items / Products
ui.caption: A partial preview of Items / Products in Adon ERP. Company, items and figures are sample data.

flow.title: How items are grouped, in four categories
flow.intro: Every item belongs to a category. The category decides which accounts it posts to, so you do not map each item by hand.

steps.question: Bought to make something
steps.body: Ink, granules, paper. Counted in stock, and moved to cost when it is used in production.

steps.question: Made and sold
steps.body: Cartons, bags, packed goods. Held in inventory until a sale moves the cost to COGS and the price to revenue.

steps.question: Used up, not sold
steps.body: Tape, gloves, cleaning supplies. Bought in bulk, with a reorder point so the shelf is never empty.

aside.body: Freight, repairs or labour. A service has no stock and no reorder level, only a price, and posts to revenue or expense.

flow.formTitle: What you fill in on a new item

form.label: Name
form.body: The only required field. Use the name your team says out loud, for example “Kraft Paper Roll”.

form.label: SKU and barcode
form.body: Your own code and an optional EAN-13 or internal barcode, so items can be found by scan or by code.

form.label: Unit of measure and cost
form.body: kg, pcs, job or your own unit, with a default unit cost that orders and bills start from.

form.label: Reorder management
form.body: Reorder point, reorder quantity, minimum and maximum stock, so low items stand out in the list.

form.label: Account mappings
form.body: Inventory, COGS, revenue and expense accounts. Optional, and filled in by the category if you leave them empty.

items.vendors: Who you buy the item from.
items.purchaseOrders: Pick items with quantity and unit cost when you order.
items.invoicesAr: Sell items to customers with their price and VAT.
items.deliveryChallans: List the items that leave the gate on each load.
items.ledgers: Inventory and cost of goods sold, account by account.
items.financialReports: Stock value and margins in your statements.
items.accountingHub: A summary of stock and sales at a glance.

local.title: An item list that fits how Bangladeshi companies trade
local.intro: Many companies buy raw material by the kilo, sell packed goods by the piece, and charge for freight as a job. One list has to handle all three.

points.title: Your own units
points.body: kg, pcs, job, roll or carton. Each item carries its unit, so quantities on orders and challans always mean the same thing.

points.title: Costs in taka
points.body: Set a default unit cost in BDT. Orders and bills start from it, and you change it when the supplier’s price moves.

points.title: Reorder points that work
points.body: Set the point once. The list shows it beside each item, so the store keeper knows what to ask for before it runs out.

faq.title: Questions we get about items

items.q: What is an item in Adon ERP?
items.a: It is anything you buy, make or sell: a product, a raw material, a consumable or a service. Each has a name, an optional SKU, a unit and a default cost.

items.q: What do I need to fill in to create an item?
items.a: Only the name is required. Add the SKU, barcode, unit, default cost and category when you have them. Everything else can be added later.

items.q: What are the item categories for?
items.a: The category sets which accounts the item posts to, so a raw material goes to inventory and a service goes to revenue without any manual mapping.

items.q: Can I set accounts for a single item?
items.a: Yes. The account mappings are optional. Leave them empty to use the category defaults, or pick your own inventory, COGS, revenue or expense account.

items.q: How do reorder points work?
items.a: Set a reorder point and quantity, with optional minimum and maximum stock. The list shows the reorder point beside each item.

items.q: Can I stop using an item without losing history?
items.a: Yes. Use Deactivate. The item leaves the pick lists but stays in old documents. The Inactive tab shows it again.

items.q: Can I export the list?
items.a: Yes. Search or filter by category, then export to CSV or Excel, print the list, or print labels.

items.q: Where is Adon ERP available?
items.a: We are currently onboarding companies in Dhaka. Book a demo and we will set up a few of your own items with you.

closing.title: Bring ten of your own items. We will set them up with units, costs and reorder points in the demo.

ui.note: Percentage-of-completion (cost-to-cost): % complete = cost to date ÷ estimated total cost (EAC); earned revenue = % × revised contract value. Over-billing = billed in excess of earned; under-billing = earned in excess of billed. This is the WIP balance-sheet adjustment.

steps.question: Spent over expected
steps.body: Cost to date divided by the estimated total cost gives the percent complete.

steps.question: Percent of the contract
steps.body: Earned revenue is the percent complete times the revised contract value.

steps.question: Against what you billed
steps.body: Billed more than earned is over-billing. Earned more than billed is under-billing.

form.body: Estimated gross profit as a share of the contract.

form.label: A balance-sheet adjustment
form.body: Over and under-billing are the WIP adjustment at period end.

meta.description: Create separate ledgers for sales, payroll, assets or projects, see how many journal entries each one holds, and keep your books easy to read. Built for companies in Bangladesh.

hero.title: Ledgers: one place for each stream of entries in your books
hero.lead: Local sales in one ledger, export in another, payroll in a third. Every journal entry is posted to a ledger, so when you open one you see only the work that belongs there, and how much of it there is.

ui.caption: A partial preview of Ledgers in Adon ERP. Company, ledger names and figures are sample data.

explain.title: What a ledger is for
explain.intro: A company with one ledger works. A company with twenty thousand entries in one ledger is hard to read. Ledgers let you group entries the way your business actually runs.

rows.label: Name
rows.question: What does this ledger hold?
rows.body: Use a name anyone in accounts would understand without asking: “Export Sales”, not “Ledger 3”. It is the name your team will pick on every new journal entry.

rows.label: JEs
rows.question: How busy is it?
rows.body: The number of journal entries posted to the ledger so far. A ledger with thousands of entries is a daily workhorse. One still at zero was probably set up for something that hasn’t started yet.

rows.label: Created
rows.question: When was it set up?
rows.body: Useful at year-end and during an audit, when someone asks why a ledger exists and since when.

rows.label: Actions
rows.question: Can we change it later?
rows.body: Rename a ledger whenever you need to. A ledger with no entries in it can also be removed, so a mistake made during setup doesn’t stay in your books.

explain.ideasTitle: Ledger ideas that work well here
explain.ideasIntro: There is no single right set. These are the splits we see most often in Bangladeshi companies.

ideas.title: Local sales and export sales
ideas.body: Export earnings are handled differently by the bank and the auditor. Keeping them apart from day one saves a lot of sorting in June.

ideas.title: Payroll
ideas.body: Salaries, festival bonuses and their accruals in one place, separate from trading entries.

ideas.title: Fixed assets
ideas.body: Machinery, vehicles and their monthly depreciation, so the asset story is easy to follow.

ideas.title: One ledger per project
ideas.body: A new warehouse, a factory floor, a large client contract. Set it up before the first taka is spent.

ideas.title: Each sister concern’s general ledger
ideas.body: Name it after the company it belongs to, so nobody posts to the wrong one by accident.

ideas.title: Fee or subscription income
ideas.body: Schools, clubs and training centres often keep collections in a ledger of their own because the volume is so high.

related.journalEntries: Every entry is posted to one of your ledgers.
related.chartOfAccounts: The accounts each journal line moves money between.
related.financialReports: Profit and loss and the balance sheet across your books.
related.accountingHub: The whole picture on one screen.

faq.title: Questions we get about ledgers

items.q: What is a ledger in Adon ERP?
items.a: It is a named book that journal entries are posted to. You choose the ledger on every new journal entry, and the Ledgers screen shows each one with how many entries it holds and when it was created.

items.q: How many ledgers should we have?
items.a: Start small. A general ledger plus one for each stream your team handles separately, such as sales, payroll or a large project, is enough for most companies. You can add more at any time.

items.q: How do I create a new ledger?
items.a: Click “New Ledger”, type a name and click “Create Ledger”. That is the whole form.

items.q: Can we rename a ledger later?
items.a: Yes. Use the edit action next to the ledger. The entries already posted to it stay where they are.

items.q: Can we delete a ledger?
items.a: A ledger with no entries can be deleted. Once entries have been posted to it, keep it and rename it if needed, so your audit trail stays complete.

items.q: Are ledgers the same as separate companies?
items.a: No. Ledgers split entries inside one company. If you run separate legal companies, set each one up as its own company and switch between them from the top bar.

items.q: Can Adon ERP print a Mushak-6.3?

items.q: How is VAT calculated on an invoice?

items.q: What do draft, approved, paid and canceled mean?
items.a: Draft is still being prepared. Approved means the buyer owes the amount. Paid means the full amount has been received. Canceled invoices stay in the list with their number, for the record.

items.q: Can a buyer pay part of an invoice?
items.a: Yes. The Paid column shows how much has come in so far, next to the full amount, so part-paid invoices are easy to spot.

items.q: Do I need to choose accounts every time?

items.q: Can I print a normal bill as well as the tax invoice?
items.a: Yes. “Print Bill” gives a commercial invoice with your letterhead, line items, total and the amount in words.

items.q: Can I export invoices?
items.a: Yes. Search the list, then export to CSV or Excel, or print it.

explain.title: Every part of the entry, and why it is there
explain.intro: A journal entry is a short form, but each field answers a question someone will ask later: you next month, your auditor next year, or a bank officer checking your accounts.

rows.label: Description
rows.question: Will this still make sense in a year?
rows.body: Write it for the person who has never seen it. “October salaries accrued, paid in November” is useful. “Adj” is not. The description is what you will search for later, so name the month and the reason.

rows.label: Ledger
rows.question: Where should this entry live?
rows.body: Choose the ledger the entry belongs to, so it shows up where your team expects to find it, next to the other entries of its kind.

rows.label: Project (optional)
rows.question: Does this cost belong to a job?
rows.body: If the entry is part of a particular project, such as a new production line or a client contract, tag it. If not, leave it on “No project”.

rows.label: Lines
rows.question: Which accounts move, and which way?
rows.body: Each line is an account, an amount and a side: Dr or Cr. Two lines cover most entries. Need more? Add a line, for example to split one salary accrual across factory, office and sales.

rows.label: The totals under the lines
rows.question: Does it balance?
rows.body: Debit and credit totals sit under the lines and update as you type. When they match, a tick appears. In double entry, every taka that goes in one side has to come out of the other.

rows.label: The list after posting
rows.question: Can we find it again?
rows.body: Posted entries are numbered by year (JE-2026-…) and listed with their totals. Search by description, then export to CSV or Excel, or print, when the auditor asks for the month’s journal.

local.title: The month-end entries every accountant in Bangladesh knows
local.intro: These come up every month in most companies here. None of them comes from an invoice or a bill, so each one is a journal entry.

points.title: Salaries owed at month-end
points.body: Workers are paid in the first week of the next month, but the cost belongs to this one. Record it in the month it was earned.
points.entry: Dr Salaries expense · Cr Salaries payable

points.title: Eid bonus, a little every month
points.body: Two festival bonuses a year are a large cost. Setting aside a share each month stops one month’s profit from collapsing before Eid.
points.entry: Dr Bonus expense · Cr Bonus provision

points.title: The electricity bill that comes late
points.body: The DESCO or DPDC bill for October arrives in November. Put the cost back in October, where it was used.

points.title: Bank charges you only see on the statement
points.body: Excise duty, SMS charges and account fees are taken directly by the bank. Record them when the statement arrives so the bank balance matches.
points.entry: Dr Bank charges · Cr Bank account

points.title: Depreciation on machinery and vehicles
points.body: The cost of a machine is spread across the years it works. One entry a month keeps profit honest and the balance sheet realistic.

points.title: Fixing a wrong posting
points.body: Rent booked to repairs? The clean habit is to reverse the wrong entry and post a correct one, both with clear descriptions, so the trail makes sense to an auditor.

faq.title: Questions we get about journal entries

items.q: What is a journal entry in Adon ERP?
items.a: It is a manual double-entry record: a description, a ledger, an optional project, and two or more lines, each with an account, an amount and a debit or credit side. You use it for anything that does not come from an invoice, bill, receipt or other tool.

items.q: When should I use a journal entry instead of an invoice or bill?
items.a: Use invoices, bills, receipts and petty cash for everyday buying, selling and paying. Use a journal entry for depreciation, accruals, provisions, bank charges you only see on the statement, and corrections.

items.q: How do I know the entry balances?
items.a: The debit total and the credit total are shown under the lines and update as you type. A tick appears when the two are equal.

items.q: Can one entry have more than two lines?
items.a: Yes. Use “Add line” to add as many as you need, for example to split one salary accrual across several departments.

items.q: Can I link an entry to a project?
items.a: Yes. The form has an optional Project field. Leave it on “No project” when the entry is not tied to one.

items.q: How are journal entries numbered?
items.a: Each entry gets a number with the year in it, such as JE-2026-004318, and appears in the Journal Entries list with its debit and credit totals and its status.

items.q: Can I give the journal to my auditor?
items.a: Yes. You can search the list, export it to CSV or Excel, or print it.

numbers.title: Five numbers, five questions an owner actually asks
numbers.intro: A dashboard is only useful if you know what to do with what it shows. Here is what each figure on the hub means, where it comes from, and when it should make you pick up the phone.

rows.label: Revenue (YTD)
rows.question: Are we selling more than we were?
rows.body: Everything invoiced since your fiscal year started. Most companies here run July to June, so by December this is about six months of sales. Compare it with the same point last year, not with last month.

rows.label: Net income
rows.question: After every cost, did we make money?
rows.body: Revenue, minus the cost of what you sold, minus salaries, rent, fuel and everything else it takes to run. When this goes negative the hub shows it in red. It does not soften bad news.

rows.label: AR outstanding
rows.question: How much of our money is sitting with buyers?
rows.body: Invoices sent and not yet paid. For a factory selling to large buyers on 60 or 90 days, this is often bigger than the bank balance, and it is the figure that decides whether salaries go out on time.

rows.label: AP outstanding
rows.question: Who are we holding up?
rows.body: Supplier bills you have accepted and not paid. A small AP next to a large AR means you are financing your customers. Worth knowing before you ask the bank for working capital.

rows.label: Total assets
rows.question: How big is this business, really?
rows.body: Cash, bank balances, stock, receivables, machinery and property, added up from the balance sheet. It is the number a lender or investor will look at first.
rows.source: the asset accounts in your Chart of Accounts

charts.title: The income statement in five bars
charts.body: Revenue, cost of goods, gross profit, running costs and net income, side by side. Gross margin sits in the corner, so you can see at a glance when raw material prices start eating into it.

charts.title: Where the running costs go
charts.body: Operating expenses split by type. In a factory, salaries are usually the biggest slice. When fuel or transport starts to grow, you see it here before you see it in the year-end accounts.

charts.title: Top five customers by what they owe
charts.body: Your call list for the week. If one name holds a third of all receivables, that is a concentration risk, and it is better to see it on a Monday morning than in an audit.

charts.title: Top five vendors by what you owe
charts.body: Who to pay first, and who you can reasonably talk to about terms. Useful the week before Eid, when every supplier wants to be paid at once.

tools.title: Seventeen tools feed the hub. You never type a number twice.
tools.intro: The hub does not hold figures of its own. Every number on it is read from the work your team already does in the tools below: an invoice raised, a cheque deposited, a bill approved.

items.billsAp: Supplier bills waiting for payment. Together they make the AP figure.
items.itemsProducts: What you buy and sell, with units and prices.
items.bankAccounts: Every account the company holds, with balances to check against the statement.
items.chequeRegister: Cheques received and issued, with their dates, so none is forgotten in a drawer.
items.pettyCash: Tea, rickshaw fare, courier. Small amounts that add up by June.
items.vatRegister: VAT on sales and VAT on purchases, side by side for the monthly return.
items.financialReports: Profit and loss, balance sheet and the statements a bank or auditor asks for.

points.title: Your fiscal year, your dates

day.title: A normal Tuesday with the hub
day.intro: How an accounts team at a mid-sized packaging factory might use it.

steps.text: The accounts head opens the hub. Receivables are up since last week, and the top-five list shows exactly which buyer is behind it.
The Cheque Register shows two cheques dated today. One goes to the bank. The other buyer asks for a week, and the call is noted.
The store sends a delivery challan for film rolls that left the gate. The invoice goes out the same afternoon, VAT included.
A resin supplier’s bill arrives and is checked against the purchase order before it is accepted.
Petty cash is counted and closed. When the owner checks the hub from home, today’s numbers are already in it.

faq.title: Questions we get about the Accounting Hub

items.q: What is the Accounting Hub in Adon ERP?
items.a: It is the first screen of the Accounting app. It shows revenue for the year so far, net income, receivables, payables and total assets, along with an income statement chart, an expense breakdown and your top customers and vendors by balance. Everything on it is live.

items.q: Where do the numbers on the hub come from?
items.a: From the work your team already records: invoices, receipts, bills, journal entries, bank and cheque records. The hub reads them from the ledgers. There is nothing to type into the hub itself, so it cannot fall out of step with the books.

items.q: Does it handle VAT in Bangladesh?
items.a: Yes. VAT is captured on invoices and bills and collected in the VAT Register, so sales VAT and purchase VAT for the month are in one place when your return is due.

items.q: Can we see amounts in lakh and crore?
items.a: Yes. Headline figures are shown in Cr and L, with the full taka amount printed underneath each one.

items.q: Can one login manage more than one company?
items.a: Yes. Group companies can switch between companies from the top bar, and each company keeps its own chart of accounts, ledgers and reports.

items.q: Is the software available in Bangla?
items.a: Yes. You can switch between English and Bangla from the top bar at any time.

items.q: Do we need an accountant to use it?
items.a: Someone who understands debits and credits should set up the chart of accounts and post journal entries. The hub itself is written for owners and managers, and does not need accounting training to read.

header.title: Quality
header.subtitle: without the complexity
header.description: Build smart quality checks, catch defects early, manage inspections, and keep production moving without adding unnecessary complexity.

dashboard.title: Quality Dashboard
dashboard.description: Non-conformance, CAPA, and inspection quality at a glance — last 90 days

nonConformance.description: From inspections, production, or customer complaints — every defect gets an NC record, a severity, and a disposition, from raising it through closure.
nonConformance.panelDescription: Track every quality defect through disposition and closure — from inspections, production, or complaints.

severity.title: Severity levels
severity.description: Minor, Major, and Critical — Critical indicates a customer safety risk, recall, or shipment hold.

rootCause.title: Root-cause methods
rootCause.description: Use 5 Whys, Fishbone (Ishikawa), 8D, or Pareto — whichever method fits the problem.

traceability.title: Full traceability
traceability.description: Every NC links to the CAPA, inspection, and shipment from which it originated.

capa.description: Drive every non-conformance to a verified, effective fix — root cause, action items, verification, and closure. Do not just fix it once; make sure it never happens again.
capa.panelDescription: Drive every non-conformance to a verified, effective fix — root cause, action items, verification, and closure.

fiveWhys.title: 5 Whys —
fiveWhys.description: ask why repeatedly (usually five times) to trace a defect back to its true cause.

fishbone.title: Fishbone (Ishikawa) —
fishbone.description: map causes across Machine, Material, Method, People, Measurement, and Environment.

eightD.title: 8D —
eightD.description: use an eight-discipline process for major customer complaints and export shipments.

pareto.title: Pareto —
pareto.description: rank defects by frequency so you address the biggest problem first.

lifecycle.openCapa: Open CAPA and assign an owner

aql.description: Enter the lot size, AQL, and inspection level — the calculator gives you the sample size and acceptance and rejection numbers. Suitable for buyer audits by H&M, Zara, Primark, Walmart, and Target.
aql.panelDescription: Acceptance sampling for buyer audits — lot size + AQL + level → sample size and acceptance/rejection.
aql.exampleDescription: Six defects among 80 samples are within the acceptance number of 10, so the lot passes and ships. If defects reach the rejection number (11 or more), the lot fails and an NC and CAPA are raised automatically.

spc.description: Statistical Process Control monitors your process while production is running — not only the finished product. Use individual and moving-range charts plus process capability (Cp/Cpk) from QC readings.
spc.panelDescription: Individual and moving-range control charts and process capability (Cp/Cpk) from QC readings.

capability.title: Cp / Cpk
capability.description: Cp shows process width versus specification. Cpk shows whether the process is centered — below 1 means it needs attention.

limits.title: UCL / LCL vs USL / LSL
limits.description: Statistical control limits differ from customer specification limits — SPC monitors both.

alerts.title: Out-of-control alerts
alerts.description: When a reading crosses a control limit, production stops for investigation before parts are rejected.

workflow.description: NC, CAPA, AQL, and SPC are connected — a failed inspection raises an NC, an NC opens a CAPA, and SPC prevents the next defect before it starts.

inspect.title: 1. Inspect
inspect.description: A QC inspection or AQL sample identifies a defect.

raiseNc.title: 2. Raise NC
raiseNc.description: The non-conformance is recorded with its severity and source.

capa.title: 3. CAPA
capa.description: The root cause is found and corrective and preventive actions are assigned.

spc.title: 4. SPC monitoring
spc.description: The process is monitored so the same defect cannot recur.

worksWithProcess.title: Works with your process
worksWithProcess.description: Add quality checks inside manufacturing, inventory, and delivery operations without slowing your team.

centralizeInspections.title: Centralize inspections
centralizeInspections.description: Create control points, quality alerts, corrective actions, and inspection history in one place.

kanbanView.title: Kanban view
kanbanView.description: Manage quality alerts by status using a clean drag-and-drop workflow.

orderIntegration.title: Order integration
orderIntegration.description: Trigger checks directly from manufacturing orders, transfers, receipts, and deliveries.

section1.title: Quality

qualityAlert.title: Quality Alert
qualityAlert.correctiveActionText: Block the faulty batch, notify supplier, and re-check components before production continues.

section3.title: No product

inspectionWorksheet.operatorNoteText: Add measurement, attach image, and validate the inspection.

section3.descriptionText: Choose product-specific checks and inspection worksheets. Track photos, measurements, pass/fail answers, and comments for every important operation.

section4.title: Put your
